Literature

Matilda Lockhart was the daughter of Sir John Lockhart. She married Lt.-Gen. James Lockhart-Wishart, 4th of Carnwath and 17th of the Lee. Her married name became Lockhart-Wishart.

In the present work, Matilda is depicted as being busy in the elegant task of knotting. It involved the use of an ornamental shuttle, often inlaid with precious metal, a reel of thread and a decorative bag in which these materials could be kept. It was a graceful occupation which looked well when done in public and the little bag could easily be carried about with its owner. At first sight the shuttle resembles the kind used for tatting, but in fact it is larger and is open at each end which a tatting shuttle is not. She would be making a trimming for either a garment or for some item of furnishing, because in knotting a plain length of yarn was decorated with knots or picots. (R.K. Marshall, Women in Scotland 1660-1780, National Galleries of Scotland, 1979, p.64).

description_block:
David Roberts RA (British, 1796-1864)
View of Donaldson's Hospital from the North West (1851) 
signed 'David Roberts RA' (lower left)
oil on canvas
128 x 190.5cm (50 3/8 x 75in).

Provenance
Commissioned by the architect W.H. Playfair.
The Donaldson's Trust.

Exhibited
Edinburgh, Royal Scottish Academy, 1852, cat.no.433, loaned by W.H. Playfair Esq.
Edinburgh, Scottish National Exhibition, 1908, loaned by Donaldson's Trust.

Literature
J. Ballantine, The Life of David Roberts, R.A., Edinburgh, 1866 p.170.

The art historian James Caw characterised David Roberts as 'the only Scottish painter of importance who has devoted himself to painting architecture...amongst British workers in the genre...he holds the foremost place.' [1] Painted at the height of Roberts' career, the present work is a spectacular view of his native Edinburgh and its appearance at this auction marks the first time in this masterpiece's 175-year history that it has been offered for sale.

David Roberts became one of the most celebrated British painters of the mid-19th century, despite beginning life in relatively humble circumstances. Born in Stockbridge, in 1796, he became apprenticed to an Edinburgh house painter and worked on theatrical sets before establishing himself as a landscape artist. Inspired by Turner, he made regular expeditions abroad and his carefully composed, atmospheric paintings conveyed both the excitement of experiencing picturesque and exotic sites with fascinating details. He soon became a rising star of British Art, as a contemporary review recognised:
'Mr Roberts is an artist possessing talents of the highest class; in his works profound art and the most scientific display of detail are equally perceptible; not as subservient the one to the other, but as co-operating to produce a perfect whole.' [2]

In 1838, following these earlier journeys through Europe, he set out on the most ambitious tour of his career, travelling through Egypt, Sinai, Petra and the Holy Land and arriving in Jerusalem the following year. On returning to Britain after each of his travels, he transformed his on-the-spot sketches and watercolours into grand, highly detailed oil canvases. Roberts' works were also used to create collections of lithographs, reproduced in deluxe folios, intended for rarefied circles of connoisseurship. The project was funded through advance subscriptions and Queen Victoria signed up as the first subscriber. Roberts' appointment as a Commissioner for the Great Exhibition of 1851, under the patronage of Prince Albert, confirmed his status. The present work was completed in the same year.

When Edinburgh printer and businessman, James Donaldson, died in 1830, he left his estate to charity. His will bequeathed 'all his property, heritable and personal ... to build and found a hospital for boys and girls, to be called Donaldson's Hospital'. Twenty years later, an impressive school building finally opened its doors at West Coates. Donaldson's School, as it came to be known, became an important part of Edinburgh's skyline.

William Henry Playfair designed the building in the Jacobethan style, built round a quadrangle in Tudor style with large corner towers which themselves are each made up of four smaller towers. As an architect at the end of his career, he must have been particularly pleased with the finished result as he commissioned Roberts to paint this masterpiece, for the princely sum of £200. When Queen Victoria officially opened the building, she is reputed to have said that the building was more impressive than many of her own palaces.

During his time in Edinburgh and London, Roberts had also developed a reputation as an architectural designer, although he narrowly missed winning the competition to design Edinburgh's Scott Monument. His skill in technical drawing, together with his royal patronage, may have prompted Playfair to commission this monumental oil painting of the newly constructed Donaldson's Hospital.

A related watercolour dated 3 October 1845, now in the National Gallery of Scotland, appears to have provided the basis for the present work. In the watercolour, Donaldson's Hospital is the sole focus and no figures appear. In the oil painting, by contrast, Roberts enlivened the foreground with washerwomen on the banks of the Water of Leith and a herd of cattle at the water's edge, separating the figures from the distant view. The combination of narrative incident, imposing architecture and distant hills, suffused with sunlight breaking through a cloudy sky, recurs to great effect across Roberts' landscapes. It was central to the reputation he built by uniting architectural grandeur with an idealised vision of rural life.

Roberts appears to have exercised some artistic licence in arranging Edinburgh's landmarks, although the general viewpoint is from the northwest of the city, with Donaldson's Hospital at its centre, beyond the building can be seen Edinburgh Castle, Arthur's Seat, Calton Hill and even North Berwick Law. Several other prominent buildings designed by Playfair also appear, including the Royal Institution building, now the Royal Scottish Academy, and the newly built National Monument of Scotland on Calton Hill.

Despite living in London, Roberts never forgot his beloved home city of Edinburgh. A few years earlier, he had painted Edinburgh from Castle Rock (Yale Centre for British Art). When exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1847, one critic felt it gave viewers "the most complete representation of the most picturesque city in the world . . . as if they had visited the city itself by railway." Robert's himself wrote in 1857 'Its dear old hill - even the Castle Rock - recalls the old times when I first tried my prentice hand on sketching, and although many sad changes have since taken place in the ancient town, the sight of it always brings with it reflections of many happy days.' [3] Another view of Edinburgh by Roberts, painted looking west from Carlton Hill was painted in 1863 and shows many of the same landmarks from the opposing view (Guildhall Art Gallery, London). 

The Donaldson's Hospital building continued to be a much-loved feature in Edinburgh's architectural history, although the use changed over the decades. In 1856 it was agreed by the governors of Donaldson's, that deaf children should not be excluded and subsequently Donaldson's developed into a resource predominately for pupils who were deaf, although hearing children were always accepted. During the Second World War it became a prisoner of war camp in Edinburgh and the school housed both German and Italian prisoners. In 2008, Donaldson's moved to a new campus in Linlithgow. It continues there today, supporting pupils with a wide range of communication needs, as the National Body for Neurodiversity. Meanwhile, the original West Coates building has been developed into luxury apartments. The building remains 'Category A' listed. Furthermore, it stands as testimony to the special architectural and historical interest of this iconic structure of one of the most beautiful cities in the world.

[2] Excerpt from The Gallery of Modern British Artists, Simpkin and Marshall, London, 1835.
[3] James Ballantine, The Life of David Roberts, R.A., 1866, p. 189.

description_block:
Sir John Lavery RA RSA RHA (Irish, 1856-1941)
A Milkmaid 
signed and dated 'J Lavery 89' (lower left)
oil on canvas
81 x 53cm (31 7/8 x 20 7/8in).

Provenance
The sitter, thence by descent.

On Friday 29 November 1889, Glasgow Art Club staged a Grand Costume Ball at St Andrew's Hall in aid of the Scottish Artists' Benevolent Association. The ball was an enormous success, attended by 967 of the most prominent citizens in the west of Scotland. It was a momentous occasion and, as A. S. Boyd later recalled, 'nothing so good of the kind had been seen in Glasgow' before that night.[1]

The evening began with a grand tableau vivant based on Paul Delaroche's frieze in the dome of the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris, known as the Hemicycle of the Arts. This involved the Glasgow Boys dressing up as great painters of the past. Lavery appeared in a satin doublet and knickerbockers as Rembrandt, James Guthrie took a prominent role as the great classical painter Apelles, Edward Arthur Walton dressed in a kimono as Hokusai, James Paterson appeared as Botticelli, and others represented Holbein and Bellini. A 'Modern Artist's Studio', painted in blue and gold, was established in a room adjacent to the Octagon Hall. During the evening, Lavery, MacGregor Wilson, A. S. Boyd, Paterson, Kennedy and Hamilton were at work making sketches in accordance with a notice displayed at the door: "A fresh old master at work every half hour". Lavery was kept busy throughout the evening, well practised in swift studies, he painted guests in their costumes.[2]

Lavery's best-known work of the evening, Hokusai and the Butterfly (National Gallery of Scotland, Edinburgh), celebrated the engagement of Walton and Helen Law. Glasgow Art Club produced a large 'souvenir' volume illustrating several sketches by the resident artists. It named works by Lavery which may have been painted afterwards from photographs and sittings, including A Milkmaid. Until recently, the present work was untraced.

The sitter for this painting was Alice Lilian Louisa Cumming, known as Lily. Lily was born in 1870, the daughter of Dr James Simpson Cumming, a general practitioner. James had been admitted to Glasgow Art Club in 1886 as one of its original lay members.
The morning after the ball, the Glasgow Herald published an article reviewing the event, calling it a 'brilliant success' and 'the most important local social function of the season'. It also listed all the attendees and their fancy dress costumes. Among the hundreds of names listed were 'Dr Cumming, 24 Blythswood Square as Gentleman, 1789. Mrs Cumming, as Lady, 1789. Miss Cumming, as Country Girl, 1789.'[3]

The year 1889 was pivotal for Lavery, one in which he honed his ability to capture likenesses quickly and cemented his position as a rising star of the art world. In late 1888, he had been contracted by Glasgow City Council to produce a large memorial canvas portraying the State Visit of Queen Victoria to its International Exhibition (Glasgow Museums). The task, which necessitated depicting a gathering of 253 guests, with visits across Scotland and to London, Windsor and Darmstadt to paint members of the royal household, was daunting. It consumed the next two years of the artist's life, requiring a move to a larger studio at West George Street, with most of the preliminary portrait sketches being painted in 1889.[4] Lavery also won a bronze medal at the Paris International Exhibition. It may seem surprising that, during the busiest year of his life, Lavery should have taken on other commissions, but such was his reputation as a Salon medallist that he was in great demand. The cachet of association with such an important young artist was clearly desirable. The present work is an excellent showcase of Lavery's signature strengths: sophisticated tonal harmony and the ability to combine fluid, dashing brushwork with structured realism and impressionistic texture.

Although Lily is depicted in the costume of a milkmaid from 1789, she was, in 1889, a thoroughly modern woman. Her pose hints at self-assurance and pride, with her hand resting confidently on her hip. When this portrait was painted, Lily was a student. Just a few years later, she and three classmates became the first women in Scotland to graduate as Bachelors of Medicine, and the first women to graduate with degrees from Glasgow University. Lily also achieved a Certificate of Midwifery and it is thought that she initially worked with her father before gaining a Doctor of Public Health certificate from the University of Cambridge in 1899. Lily remained connected with the medical profession after having children, including occasional work as an anaesthetist at Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge, advising women on reproductive health and family planning with a view to their being able to avoid unwanted pregnancies, and, before and during the First World War, involvement in Red Cross nursing examinations and charity organisation work. When Lily died in 1945, the painting remained in her family by descent and had been on loan to the Hunterian since 2018. This auction marks the first time the work has been seen in public.

[3] The Glasgow Herald, Saturday 30 November 1889, p.9.

Girl in a Cloche Hat

Exhibited
Edinburgh, Aitken Dott & Son (The Scottish Gallery), Recent Acquisitions, April-May 1977, cat.no.71.

Leslie Hunter's romantic relationships were somewhat of a mystery to his friends and family. He rarely spoke of such things and yet throughout his life it appears he had many relationships, leaving behind numerous paintings of potential companions. 

This compelling painting is one of the earliest examples of Hunter's growing development in modernist expression. Dating from 1920 to 1921, it is confirmation not of a detailed likeness in the traditional form of portraiture but of Hunter's search for how to capture in paint the essence of a person's being. Luscious use of paint for form, no direct light, and a richly coloured but indeterminate background has adeptly captured this young woman's natural allure in her time and place. 

Bonhams would like to thank Jill Marriner for her assistance with this footnote.

description_block:
John Maclauchlan Milne RSA (British, 1885-1957)
Summer Seas, Iona 
signed 'Maclauchlan Milne' (lower left)
watercolour and charcoal
27 x 38cm (10 5/8 x 14 15/16in).

Provenance
Private collection, UK, thence by descent.

It was rare for John Maclauchlan Milne to write the titles of his paintings on the reverse. In March 1933 he learnt that, after several attempts, he had been elected as an Associate of the Royal Scottish Academy (RSA). This coincided with his exhibition in Dundee with friends and fellow artists Stewart Carmichael and Alec Grieve. Milne's work was already framed and some of the pieces had been offered at his studio exhibition in October the previous year. To mark his progress at the RSA, he added the title and his signature (with his new ARSA designation) to some of his paintings on the reverse.

Local hotel records confirm that Milne stayed on the island of Iona in 1937, 1938 and 1939. The first of his Iona paintings were included in his solo exhibition at the Pearson & Westergaard gallery in Glasgow in September-October 1937.

In February 1937 he learnt that he had been elected as an academician of the RSA. As in 1933, he added the title and his signature to the reverse of these Iona watercolours, possibly to emphasise his new professional status (and to add value to his work). A watercolour entitled Summer Seas, Iona was exhibited at the Society of Scottish Artists (no. 121, 10 Dec. 1937 to 22 Jan. 1938).

The titles Summer Seas, Iona and Sound of Iona were used by Milne on different oils and watercolours including those exhibited at the RSA in 1938, and at the Royal Glasgow Institute (RGI) in 1938 and '39.

Milne's 50-year career as a professional artist can be divided into distinct periods, such as Paris in the early 1920s, then the Côte d'Azur, then the Scottish Highlands in the mid-1930s, before Iona in the late-1930s and the final phase on Arran. These two watercolours are typical of his paintings from the North End of the island and reminiscent of works by his fellow colourists S.J. Peploe and F.C.B. Cadell.

John Maclauchlan Milne RSA (British, 1885-1957)
Sannox Bay 
signed 
oil on board
61 x 51cm (24 x 20 1/16in).

Provenance
Private collection, Canada (likely acquired in the 1960's), thence by descent.

The present work is a fine example of Milen's Arran paintings. Sannox Bay is less than 3 miles from where John Maclauchlan Milne lived at High Corrie, north of Brodick, on the east coast of the island of Arran. He first visited Arran in 1939 and his studio exhibition in Dundee in April 1940 included his paintings of Iona and Arran. From 1939, his exhibits at the Royal Scottish Academy and at the Royal Glasgow Institute included many Arran pictures.

Sometime in 1940/41, after more than 30 years, he finally left Dundee and he would live on Arran until near the end of his life in October 1957. Initially he lived in a boarding house at the northern end of the village of Corrie, but after meeting the woman who became his second wife, they lived at Seaview in High Corrie.

Most, possibly all, of Milne's Arran paintings are from locations within about 3 miles of High Corrie and he painted his colourist landscapes from Brodick Bay to Glen Sannox. Sannox Bay was a favourite location.

Exhibited
London, Alex Reid & Lefevre Ltd, New Paintings by Anne Redpath, March 2962.

Anne Redpath's exhibition in the Spring of 1962 at Alex Reid & Lefevre Ltd in London was a huge success with everything selling soon after opening. The Manchester City Art Gallery sent a curator down to London to choose a painting, but had been disappointed to find everything had sold (P Bourne, Anne Redpath 1895-1965: Her Life and Work, Edinburgh, 1989, p.94).

Redpath commented in 1961: 'I think that I have always been interested in the textural quality of paint and painting and I think what I have got out of different countries like the Canary Islands, Corsica, Brittany and Portugal is something structural. So you see I haven't gone really away from depicting the object although it has a kind of abstraction...I would go to Corsica and paint houses on a hill-side. I would exaggerate the buttress quality of the building...instead of having it at right angles to the earth I would exaggerate the fact that the base of it was broader than the top of it, then therefore it looked as if it was growing out of the hill. So that while I am interested in the structural shapes of the picture, I am also interested in the structure of the objects themselves. And therefore they are really more convincing than they were before.' (as quoted by Philip Long, Anne Redpath 1895-1965, National Galleries of Scotland, Edinburgh, exh. cat., 1996, p. 26).

description_block:
Anne Redpath OBE RSA ARA LLD ARWS ROI RBA (British, 1895-1965)
Market - Gran Canaria 
signed 'Anne Redpath' (lower right)
oil on board
55.8 x 91.5 cm. (22 x 36 in.)

Provenance
Gifted by the artist to Dr Ralph Kauntze, thence by descent. 

Literature
P Bourne, Anne Redpath 1895-1965: Her Life and Work, Edinburgh, 1989, p.89.

Anne Redpath is one of the most important Scottish artists of the twentieth century. Painted on a large-scale board, with a powerful and richly intense palette, the present work reflects the confidence of her later work. Pure vibrant colour has been used to convey the heat of the sun radiating off the buildings and parasols in this bustling marketplace. Gifted by Redpath to her doctor, it has remained in the same family for over 6 decades. 

Patrick Bourne retells the story in his major Redpath biography:
'While she was in London for the opening of her second exhibition at the Lefevre Gallery in 1959, Anne Redpath suffered a second coronary thrombosis. She had never lost the feeling that in London she was showing to strangers, exposing new and untried work to a more demanding audience than she knew at home, and this must have been a contributory factor. She was taken to Nuffield House, the private wing of Guy's Hospital, where she remained for five weeks. Dr Ralph Kauntze, her consultant physician, remembers her well as "a splendid patient who showed great bravery. She was also most unusual in that she contemplated her future with great detachment." Apart from Alastair and Lindsay she was not allowed any visitors. Doctor's orders forbade painting or even drawing; these she observed without complaint.

Privately Dr Kauntze thought that his patient could not expect to live for more than three years. Despite the fact that she never broached the subject with him, he had the impression that she knew this to be the case. Before she left hospital Redpath said that she was going to produce a painting for the doctor. A few months later Alastair delivered to Dr Kauntze's London home to his great delight a painting she had completed for him, which in typically generous manner was a much more important work than he might have anticipated.

The Scottish Gallery's 1960 Edinburgh Festival Exhibition was 'Gran Canaria Paintings by Anne Redpath'. The catalogue contained only twenty-one works, all oil paintings of the Canary Islands, which she had visited the previous February with Lindsay. Whereas the paintings from the Spanish and Corsican visits had in some cases gestated in her mind for as long as four years, the Canary paintings came to fruition more quickly. It was as though she knew that, following her recent illness, she no longer had the luxury of prolonged reflection. This was her first exhibition on a single theme. It was a considerable success, not least because she had painted the landscape of the islands in different moods, giving the exhibition variety and balance. In The Scotsman Sydney Goodsir Smith enthused that ...the best of them are the best Anne Redpaths I have seen'. He went on to say that these Canary Island landscapes were so good that she should not paint any more table-tops because they were not worthy of her talent.'
(P Bourne, Anne Redpath 1895-1965: Her Life and Work, Edinburgh, 1989, p.89).

Jack Vettriano OBE Hon LLD (British, 1951-2025)
Cheating Hearts 
signed 'VETTRIANO' (lower left)
oil on canvas
61 x 50.8cm (24 x 20in).

Provenance
Sale; McTears, Glasgow, 3 May 2015, lot 2484.
Private collection, UK (acquired from the above).

The present work depicts a scene from the 1867 novel Thérèse Raquin, by the French writer Émile Zola. Vettriano draws direct inspiration from Zola's dark psychological novel. He captures the moody, secretive, and tense atmosphere reminiscent of the illicit passion and betrayal between the characters in this story about adultery and murder.
